title: Catherine and the pope
hook: a young laywoman writes to the pope in Avignon and urges him back to Rome
carry: if you are what you should be

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian at her window, and Margery outside it. Your line was counsel at the window. Did you get to listen to someone, really listen? Day eight hundred thirty-one.

The pope doesn't live in Rome. For a long stretch of years, the popes have lived in Avignon, in the south of France, in a great palace far from the city of Peter and Paul. In Italy, a young woman from Siena, the daughter of a wool dyer, has decided this is wrong. She holds no office. She has no title. She isn't a nun in a convent; she lives a life of prayer and service as a laywoman, one of Dominic's lay sisters, in her family's house. And she starts writing letters. To princes. To cardinals. And to the pope himself, telling him, warmly and without flinching, to come home. Today: Catherine and the pope.

Catherine of Siena couldn't easily write, the old accounts say, so she dictated. Her letters went out in Italian, the language she spoke, and they are still read today. They're bold. She calls the pope by a tender family word, something like dear father, and in the same letter tells him plainly that he must be brave, stop hesitating, and return to Rome. She doesn't flatter him. She doesn't insult him either. She speaks to him as a Christian speaking to another Christian who happens to hold enormous power, and she reminds him what that power is for. She went further than letters. She traveled to Avignon herself and spoke with him there. And the pope did return to Rome. How much of that was Catherine's doing, historians weigh differently, and the return didn't end the church's troubles; a painful split came soon after. Today the Catholic Church honors her as a saint and a Doctor of the Church. There's a saying handed down under her name, usually given in English like this: if you are what you should be, you will set the whole world on fire. It's not a slogan about being impressive. It's about being true to what you were made for. Jesus says something with the same heat in the Gospel of Luke, in the King James Bible: "I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?" In these letters, Catherine's fire was ink, and honesty, and love that wouldn't stay quiet in front of power.

Here's the practice: write to someone in power. Not the whole thing; for now, just begin it in your head. Who holds power over something you care about? A local official. A school board. A manager. A landlord. Let one name come. Then find your first honest sentence, the way Catherine might: respectful, warm, and clear about what needs to change. No insults. No flattery. Just the truth, said kindly. If you pray, you can ask for courage and for the right words. If you don't, just let the sentence settle until it sounds like you. The bell holds the time.
Catherine and the pope. A laywoman from Siena who wrote and spoke to the pope in Avignon, warmly and without fear, urging him to return to Rome.
Your line: if you are what you should be. Today, send the letter, the email or the message you began, and keep it as warm and as honest as Catherine's. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and her letters and her book, the Dialogue, are still read; some Christians who speak up to leaders in church and state look to her example.

notes: Index hook says she 'persuades him back to Rome'; the script says the pope returned and that historians weigh her role differently. The hook field was softened to 'urges'. Confirm.
Claims rule: No dates used (Gregory XI's return, 1377, and the Western Schism, 1378, are not dated or named).
'Couldn't easily write, the old accounts say, so she dictated': confirm; tradition also says she learned to write late.
'A tender family word, something like dear father': her letters address Gregory XI as 'babbo' / 'dolce babbo mio'; confirm before adding the Italian.
The carry's saying is widely attributed to her (often traced to a letter); its exact source and wording should be checked. It is paraphrased and labeled 'handed down under her name'.
'Daughter of a wool dyer' and 'a Doctor of the Church' are standard biography; confirm. 'Lives as a laywoman' — she was a Dominican tertiary (Mantellata); confirm 'not a nun in a convent' framing.
Trapdoor reworded to avoid a superlative.
Editor: fixed a garbled practice line ('Not now, in full') and toned down 'astonishing'.

Auditor: cut 'Catherine's fire wasn't a sword', which a historian would catch (her letters to Gregory XI also urged a crusade); cut the unsourced 'partly for this courage' (the Doctor title, 1970, rests on her teaching); named her as one of Dominic's lay sisters (Mantellata), linking day 819 and answering the earlier note.
